interactions.label: What defines a medicine as 'essential' according to the WHO framework?

params.question: What defines a medicine as 'essential' according to the WHO framework?

answers.text: It is manufactured by WHO-approved pharmaceutical companies

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: WHO does not approve manufacturers for the Essential Medicines List. Selection is based on public health criteria: disease prevalence, evidence of efficacy and safety, and comparative cost-effectiveness.

answers.text: It is available over the counter without a prescription in most countries

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Prescription status is not a selection criterion. WHO defines essential medicines by their ability to satisfy priority health care needs, selected based on disease prevalence, proven efficacy and safety, and comparative cost-effectiveness.

answers.text: It satisfies the priority health care needs of the population, selected based on disease prevalence, efficacy, safety, and cost-effectiveness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. WHO defines essential medicines as those that satisfy priority health care needs of the population, selected with due regard to disease prevalence, evidence of efficacy and safety, and comparative cost-effectiveness — criteria established with the first Model List in 1977.

answers.text: It is listed in every country's national pharmacopoeia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not every essential medicine appears in all national pharmacopoeias. The WHO Model List is a reference that countries adapt — selection is based on disease prevalence, efficacy, safety, and cost-effectiveness, not pharmacopoeial inclusion.

overallFeedback.feedback: Essential medicines are defined by WHO as those satisfying priority health care needs, selected based on three criteria: disease prevalence, evidence of efficacy and safety, and comparative cost-effectiveness.

Well done. These evidence-based criteria have guided the WHO Model List since its inception in 1977, when the first edition contained 208 medicines for the most prevalent health conditions in low-resource settings.

interactions.label: Why does WHO emphasise that the complementary list of essential medicines is NOT

params.question: Why does WHO emphasise that the complementary list of essential medicines is NOT a 'second tier' of importance?

answers.text: Because complementary medicines are more expensive and require special budgeting

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cost is not the reason for the distinction. WHO classifies both lists as equally essential — the complementary list simply requires referral infrastructure and specialist management, not lesser clinical priority.

answers.text: Because both lists are equally essential — the complementary list only requires referral infrastructure, not lesser clinical priority

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. WHO states that both core and complementary lists represent equally essential medicines. The distinction is purely operational: complementary medicines require specialist care or more complex management infrastructure, not that they are less important.

answers.text: Because complementary list medicines have stronger evidence of efficacy than core list medicines

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The evidence standard is the same for both lists. The complementary list differs only in requiring specialist care or referral infrastructure — it does not reflect a higher evidence threshold.

answers.text: Because the complementary list is mandatory for all countries while the core list is optional

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neither list is mandatory — both serve as reference models for national adaptation. The complementary list is equally essential because its medicines address priority conditions that happen to need specialist management, not because of different implementation obligations.

overallFeedback.feedback: WHO emphasises that the complementary list is equally essential to the core list. The only difference is operational: complementary medicines require specialist care or referral infrastructure — they are not less important clinically.
Well done. Understanding this distinction prevents the common misconception that 'complementary' means 'optional' or 'less important' in the essential medicines framework.

interactions.label: A PHC medical officer finds that amlodipine (listed in the NLEM) is out of stock

params.question: A PHC medical officer finds that amlodipine (listed in the NLEM) is out of stock. What is the correct course of action?

answers.text: Advise the patient to return when the next supply arrives

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Delaying treatment is clinically unacceptable. The medical officer should immediately substitute with another appropriate formulary medicine, document the change, and report the stock-out to generate the restocking demand signal.

answers.text: Prescribe a branded alternative from a private pharmacy without documenting the stock-out

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Omitting stock-out documentation means the supply chain receives no demand signal for amlodipine. The correct approach is to substitute within the formulary, document the change, and report the stock-out to the supply chain officer.

answers.text: Switch to a non-formulary antihypertensive to avoid treatment delay

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Non-formulary medicines bypass the evidence-based selection framework. The correct approach is to substitute with another appropriate formulary medicine using the P-drug principle, document the change, and report the stock-out.

answers.text: Substitute with an appropriate formulary alternative, document the substitution, and report the stock-out

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When an NLEM medicine is unavailable, the PHC medical officer substitutes using the P-drug approach, documents the change, and reports the stock-out to the supply chain officer — this generates the demand signal needed for restocking.

overallFeedback.feedback: When an NLEM medicine is out of stock, the PHC medical officer should substitute with an appropriate formulary alternative, document the substitution, and report the stock-out to the supply chain officer to generate the restocking demand signal.
Well done. This three-step approach — substitute, document, report — keeps treatment continuous while feeding the supply chain the demand signal it needs to prevent future shortages.
